c.tagline: Iran's clerical heart and shrine city, home to Fatima Masumeh.

taxi.fareNote: Agency taxis are metered; shared line ('khatti') taxis run fixed per-route fares - agree the price before boarding. Foreign bank cards do not work in Iran because of sanctions, so carry cash (rial); the Snapp and Tapsi apps are the easiest way to get a fair, fixed fare.

emergency.note: Fire: 125. English-speaking operators are not guaranteed; hotel or seminary staff can help. Women are required to wear a headscarf, and this is enforced strictly in this conservative shrine city.

solo.f: very conservative city — strict modest dress

avoid.reason: No dangerous districts, but non-Muslims must not enter the inner sanctuary chambers of the Hazrat-e Masumeh shrine (outer courtyards are visitable, ideally with a guide).
Dress and behave very conservatively around the shrine, and ask before photographing pilgrims or clerics to avoid offense.

hood_desc: The bustling heart around the Fatima Masumeh Shrine, ringed by the bazaar, seminaries, pilgrim hotels and religious bookshops; the classic, everything-on-foot base for a Qom visit.
An outlying district southeast of the centre built around the vast Jamkaran Mosque, a major pilgrimage site with huge open plazas; devotional and quieter than the shrine core.
A planned district in southern Qom that serves as the city's academic and seminary quarter, home to universities and many resident clerics; modern, residential and calm.
The historic covered bazaar and traditional lanes just south of the shrine, best for handicrafts, carpets, prayer stones and sohan (Qom's saffron-and-pistachio brittle).

water.note: Qom's tap water is notably salty and brackish; drink bottled or filtered water like the locals.

transit.pay: Buses and BRT are paid with a rechargeable local transit card or cash; foreign bank cards do not work anywhere in Iran, so keep rial on hand. Shared line taxis are paid per seat in cash.
transit.hours: Buses and BRT run roughly 5:30am-11pm; no overnight service, so Snapp/Tapsi ride-hailing fills the late-night gap.
transit.note: Qom has no metro; getting around means BRT and city buses, shared taxis, or ride-hailing apps. Buses have a separate women's section, and the shrine district itself is a compact walkable zone.

air: No commercial airport in Qom; nearest is Tehran Imam Khomeini International Airport (IKA), ~110 km north
train: Qom railway station on the Tehran-south main line; a high-speed Tehran-Qom-Isfahan line is under construction
bus: Qom bus terminal - frequent intercity coaches to Tehran, Isfahan, Kashan and Mashhad

transit.m: Direct intercity bus or shared taxi from IKA to Qom (~1-1.5 hr)
Private car transfer to Qom (~1 hr 10 min)

tip.r: Rounding up is appreciated in taxis and restaurants; upscale venues may add a service charge. Tipping is not deeply ingrained but is increasingly common in tourist-facing places.

food.name: Sohan
food.desc: Qom's signature saffron brittle: a golden disc of wheat-sprout toffee studded with pistachio and almond, perfumed with cardamom and rosewater.

places.name: Haj Khalifeh Ali Rahbar
places.note: The city's most famous sohan house, making the sweet for generations; the benchmark tin.

places.name: Sohan shops on Eram Street
places.note: A whole street of competing sohan makers offering samples before you buy.

places.name: Bazaar-e Bozorg-e Qom
places.note: Confectioners sell fresh-made sohan by weight, usually cheaper than the shrine-front shops.

food.name: Chelo kabab koobideh
food.desc: Minced lamb and beef kababs grilled over charcoal and served with saffron-buttered rice, grilled tomato, sumac and raw onion.

places.name: Alborz Restaurant
places.note: One of the best-known kabab houses on Qom's main restaurant strip.

places.name: Arg Salariyeh Restaurant
places.note: Traditional dining room with raised takht seating; a family favourite for grills.

places.name: Mortazavi Restaurant
places.note: Long-running Persian restaurant popular with pilgrims for its rice and kabab plates.

food.name: Dizi (abgusht)
food.desc: Lamb, chickpea and potato stew cooked in a stone crock; you drink the broth first, then mash the solids into a paste eaten with flatbread.

places.name: Yazdanpanah Historical House
places.note: Restored traditional house serving dizi and Persian classics in a courtyard setting.

places.name: Dizi houses on Al-Ghadir Boulevard
places.note: Cluster of specialist dizi bars where the crock and pounder come to the table.

places.name: Arg Salariyeh Restaurant
places.note: Serves dizi at lunch on traditional takht platforms, the way locals eat it.

food.name: Ash-e reshteh
food.desc: Thick green soup of herbs, beans and noodles finished with fried mint, crisp onion and tart kashk whey; a street staple year-round.

places.name: Ash stalls around Astane Square
places.note: Cauldrons of ash ladled to order for pilgrims; cheapest and freshest in the afternoon.

places.name: Bazaar-e Bozorg-e Qom
places.note: Traditional ash and halim counters tucked among the bazaar's food lanes.

places.name: Yazdanpanah Historical House
places.note: Sit-down version of ash reshteh alongside other traditional Persian dishes.

food.name: Chelo mahicheh
food.desc: Lamb shank slow-braised with saffron until it falls off the bone, served over buttered rice; the celebration dish of Qom's restaurants.

places.name: Mortazavi Restaurant
places.note: Known locally for its chelo mahicheh, ordered ahead on busy pilgrimage days.

places.name: Arg Salariyeh Restaurant
places.note: Large traditional restaurant where slow-cooked lamb is a menu highlight.

places.name: Alborz Restaurant
places.note: Also does chelo mahi, rice with fried fish, especially around Nowruz.

food.name: Halim
food.desc: Breakfast porridge of pounded wheat and shredded lamb or turkey, served warm with sugar, cinnamon and a pool of melted butter.

places.name: Breakfast counters near Hazrat Masumeh
places.note: Open from before dawn for pilgrims; sold out by mid-morning.

places.name: Bazaar-e Bozorg-e Qom
places.note: Traditional halim and kaleh-pacheh shops inside the bazaar's morning food lane.

places.name: Yazdanpanah Historical House
places.note: Traditional-house setting for a leisurely Persian breakfast.

food.name: Chai with nabat
food.desc: Strong Persian black tea poured from a samovar into slim glasses, sweetened by sucking it through saffron rock candy rather than stirring in sugar.

places.name: Tea stands in the Hazrat Masumeh courtyards
places.note: Free or near-free tea for pilgrims; the most atmospheric glass in the city.

places.name: Yazdanpanah Historical House
places.note: Courtyard teahouse service with qalyan-free traditional seating.

places.name: Bazaar-e Bozorg-e Qom teahouses
places.note: Old chaikhaneh counters where traders take tea and nabat through the day.

food.name: Doogh
food.desc: Salted yoghurt drink flecked with dried mint, sometimes lightly carbonated; the standard cooling partner to a plate of kabab.

places.name: Alborz Restaurant
places.note: House doogh served in jugs with the grill plates.

places.name: Arg Salariyeh Restaurant
places.note: Traditional bottled and house doogh alongside dizi and kabab.

places.name: Mortazavi Restaurant
places.note: Chilled mint doogh poured with every rice-and-meat order.

landmarks: Fatima Masumeh Shrine
Iran's second-holiest shrine, a dazzling complex of golden dome, turquoise minarets and mirrored halls entombing the sister of Imam Reza.
Jamkaran Mosque
A vast pilgrimage mosque on the city's edge, its green-lit domes drawing huge Tuesday-night crowds who leave petitions at the sacred well.
Grand Bazaar of Qom
A vaulted Qajar-era marketplace threading toward the shrine, famous for silk carpets, religious wares and the city's celebrated sohan brittle.
Feyziyeh Seminary
The historic madrasa at the heart of Shia scholarship, its graceful courtyard and iwans central to modern Iranian religious and political history.
Jameh Mosque of Qom
The city's venerable Friday mosque, founded in the 12th century, layering Seljuk, Safavid and Qajar craftsmanship around a serene courtyard.
Gonbad-e Sabz (Green Dome Mausoleums)
A quiet garden of three medieval tomb towers with conical and pyramidal domes, sheltering 14th-century stucco masterpieces.
Ayatollah Marashi Najafi Library
One of the Islamic world's greatest manuscript libraries, safeguarding tens of thousands of rare Qurans, codices and lithographs.
Astan Museum of Qom
The shrine's treasury museum, glittering with centuries of donated carpets, illuminated Qurans, coins and precious doors from the holy complex.
Historic House of Imam Khomeini
The modest home where Ayatollah Khomeini lived and taught before exile, preserved as a place of pilgrimage in the Yakhchal Qazi quarter.
Namak Lake (Daryacheh-ye Namak)
A vast blinding-white salt lake east of Qom, its cracked polygonal crust and mirages making an otherworldly desert excursion.

dom.op: Raja Passenger Trains (Islamic Republic of Iran Railways)

train.note: Qom sits on the main line running south from Tehran, so trains towards Isfahan, Shiraz, Yazd, Kerman, Bandar Abbas and Ahvaz call here, and there are connections east to Mashhad. Most are through services rather than trains that start in Qom, which means seats can be scarce and departure times awkward; the station is on the northern edge of town. Booking through Raja at https://www.raja.ir/ usually requires an Iranian bank card and an Iranian IP address, so foreigners tend to buy at the station or through an agency. Iran has no international trains from Qom - the only cross-border passenger service is the twice-weekly Van-Tabriz-Tehran train from Turkey, which resumed in March 2025 and does not come this way.

bus.note: Qom's main bus terminal is on the ring road and coaches leave for Tehran every 20-30 minutes, covering the 150 km in around 2 hours, which is faster and far more frequent than the train; Isfahan is about 4 hours and Mashhad a long overnight haul. Tickets are bought at the company counters at the terminal or through Iranian booking apps that generally need an Iranian card. No scheduled international coach starts in Qom, though during Arbaeen enormous numbers of chartered pilgrim buses run from Qom to the Mehran border for Najaf and Karbala, arranged through religious travel agencies rather than sold as ordinary tickets.

ferry.note: Qom stands on the edge of the central Iranian desert beside a seasonal salt river and is hundreds of kilometres from any sea, so no ferry or boat services exist.

half.name: Kashan
half.blurb: A desert city about an hour and a half south preserves restored 19th-century merchant mansions and the Persian garden of Bagh-e Fin.

half.name: Tehran
half.blurb: Iran's capital lies about an hour and a half north, with the Golestan Palace, Grand Bazaar, and National Museum among its major sights.

half.name: Mahallat
half.blurb: A town roughly an hour and a half southwest is built around natural hot springs used in bathhouses and small spa hotels.

full.name: Isfahan
full.blurb: A historic Persian city about three hours south centers on the vast Naqsh-e Jahan Square, ringed by mosques, palaces, and a covered bazaar.
